items.why: The explicit negation distinguishes failing to reform from appointing priests again.
The man of God declared the message, but the question’s two uses of “he” blur him with the current speaker.
The closing summary credits all four defeats to David and his men, while Jonathan kills only one.
The prediction is addressed to the officer, making him the person later trampled.
The sons saddle the donkey, but the old prophet mounts it.
The first covenant includes the Lord, king, and people; only the second is between king and people.
Jotham’s succession follows the burial, whereas Isaiah’s recording is mentioned earlier.
The passage explicitly says Uzziah was eager to leave because the Lord had afflicted him.
In the king’s reconstruction, capture is followed by entering the city, while leaving camp happens earlier.
They reject entering the famine-stricken city and decide to surrender at the Aramean camp.
The ordered battle accounts place Sibbekai’s killing before Elhanan’s.
“The news” is a vague label rather than a complete account of what was reported.
Jeroboam issues the command against the man of God, not against himself.
Uzziah enters first, and Azariah with the eighty priests follows him.
The quoted plan assigns the speaker’s child to today and the other woman’s child to tomorrow.
Zechariah instructs Uzziah, while Amaziah is only the father whose conduct Uzziah follows.
Elisha’s direct reply to the officer’s doubt is that he will see the food but not eat it.
The stated reason is the Lord’s prohibition, not dissatisfaction with the size of the offer.
After eating, Paul talks until daylight and then leaves.
Mobilizing the army precedes marching to and besieging Samaria.
Jehoiada distributes the weapons; David is identified only as their former owner.
The commander orders Paul’s accusers to present their case, not the Sanhedrin.
The people take Uzziah in order to make him king; Amaziah’s death supplies the circumstance, not the purpose.
The 307,500 men are explicitly under the 2,600 family leaders, while Jeiel and Maaseiah handle the muster.
The departing man of God meets the lion; the other prophet remains the one who saddled his donkey.
The officer is the clear referent of “him,” though this substantially duplicates Q89C41’s event.
The three on-duty companies receive separate posts, while the two normally off duty guard the temple for the king.
The letter heading identifies Claudius Lysias as sender and Felix as recipient.
Abishai rescues David by killing Ishbi-Benob, the Philistine threatening him.
After condemning their concealment, the men decide to report immediately to the palace.
Paul says the young man has information for the commander; Paul merely sends him.
The messengers return and report immediately before the people plunder the camp.
The repeated singular subject is Uzziah, but the question’s “explains the farm work” phrasing is somewhat artificial.
The speaker says “my son” was cooked first and the other woman then hid her own son.
The king requests prayer, but the man of God performs the intercession.
God helps Uzziah against three named groups; the Ammonites instead bring him tribute.
The prophet first brings the body to his city and only afterward places it in his tomb.
Joash is hidden with his nurse; his father Ahaziah is already dead.
The passage directly links the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death, not merely to the people’s rejoicing.
The commander addresses two centurions, who must prepare the much larger detachment.
The Arameans think the hired Hittite and Egyptian kings will attack; Israel’s king is only the supposed hirer.
The “murderer” sends the messenger and is called his master, identifying the king.
In the old prophet’s alleged message, “him” is the man of God who is to return and eat.
The passage causally connects Paul’s long speech to his planned departure the next day.
The original soldiers return after letting the cavalry continue with Paul.
The possessed man beats the seven sons, who then flee naked and bleeding.
Only the evil spirits are said to leave, but “on the items’ arrival” is an unnatural description absent from the passage.
The Sanhedrin is to petition, while the commander is the person expected to bring Paul.
The practitioners first assemble the scrolls and then burn them; valuation follows afterward.
The explicit sword order targets followers, but the woman is also put to death shortly afterward, making the stem potentially ambiguous.
Hearing the noise causes Athaliah to go; she sees the king only after arriving.
The conspirators are explicitly waiting for the commander’s consent before proceeding with the ambush.
The old prophet addresses the man of God and warns that the addressee’s body will lack ancestral burial.
The prophecy’s “he” refers to the newly named son Josiah, not Jeroboam at the altar.
